content.summary_of_the_paper:
This manuscript introduces GT test, which is an extension to the traditional WL test but characterizes the expressive power of
various graph Transformers. Using the GT test, the authors develop a generalized theoretical framework on structural encodings
that determines the expressivity of graph Transformers. The authors then propose a provably more powerful encoding method SPIS. Synthetic and real-world experiments demonstrate that SPIS's expressive power.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- The proposed GT test sounds novel to me and it looks very interesting. The most intriguing part is that the GT test have the potential to analyze beyond the WL test.

- It seems to me that the important part is structure encoding for dealing with GT test. In this sense, how do we analyze the expressive power of GNN with structure encoding?

- The improvement of the produced SPIS looks quite marginal from the real world dataset. And regarding the complex nature of SPIS, it might not be very useful in real applications.

- The authors listed several example structure encodings (sec 4.1), but I didn't see any further discussion about them.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- What is the runtime complexity analysis of SPIS with respect to SPD?

- Can the authors discuss position encodings as well?
content.summary_of_the_review: A novel paper with sound and thorough discussions

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer bVgE
content.comment:
Thanks for your positive feedback. Here we would like to answer your questions:

> It seems to me that the important part is structure encoding for dealing with GT test. In this sense, how do we analyze the expressive power of GNN with structure encoding?

Given Theorem 4, we can conclude that the expressivity of GNNs with absolute structural encodings can be analyzed with GT test with corresponding absolute encoding and $\text{Neighbor}_R$ relative encoding. The same task for GNNs with more complex relative structural encodings can be done similarly by replacing $\text{Neighbor}_R$ with the corresponding encoding.

> The authors listed several example structure encodings (sec 4.1), but I didn't see any further discussion about them.

We have discussed $\textit{Neighbor}$ as a characterization of the expressivity of WL in Section 4.3, and $\text{SPD}$ is deeply analyzed in Section 5.1.

> What is the runtime complexity analysis of SPIS with respect to SPD?

We have discussed it in Appendix C, and the conclusion is that the both methods have approximately $O(n^3)$ complexity.

> Can the authors discuss position encodings as well?

From our perspective, position encodings in sequence Transformers are like structural encodings on linear graphs, so their expressivity can also be compared with the proposed framework. We look forward to study them in the future.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper deals with learning for graphs, e.g., graph classification, via graph transformers. The author's contribution is two-fold. First, they establish a new test for isomorphism testing, the GT-test, that is more powerful than the 1-WL due to absolute and relative structural encodings that are aggregated alongside the node labels of a given graph. The authors further show that various graph Transformer architectures simulate the GT-test, similar to standard message-passing neural networks that simulate the 1-WL [1]. As a second contribution, the authors discuss a set of possible structural encodings showing that SGD-GT, the GT-test encoding shortest path lengths, is strictly more expressive than the 1-WL.
Further, they show that Neighbor-GT, the GT-test encoding whether two nodes are neighbors, is as expressive as the 1-WL. Lastly, the authors propose a new structural encoding called SPIS, which is more powerful than SGD-GT and can distinguish indistinguishable graphs by 3-WL. Lastly, the authors empirically validate their theoretical results, showing the superiority of the SPIS-encoding over SGD and Neighbor on various graph learning datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
- The authors provide a framework for understanding the expressive power of GNNs through the lens of structural encodings, which can serve as a basis for the theoretical analysis of a wider variety of GNN architectures.
- Thorough theoretical analysis of the discussed structural encodings, both with respect to 1-WL and each other.
Insightful comparison of 1-WL, SPD-GT, and SPIS-GT on a synthetic dataset, with respect to the number of indistinguishable graphs for each test.

**Weaknesses:**
- Since the main practical contribution of this work is the SPIS encoding, it would be interesting to see how the encoding fares with Transformer approaches other than Graphormer.
- The experiment results should be extended to MPNNs augmented with the discussed structural encodings, as the proposed GT-test is not limited to Transformers.

**Suggestions and remarks**
- The proposed GT test is more or less the standard 1-WL as used in the theory community, which considers neighbors as well as non-neighbors. The 1-WL as used in the ML community is actually called color refinement; see, e.g., https://people.cs.umass.edu/~immerman/pub/opt.pdf.
- Theorem 4 is not new and widely known in the theory community, see, e.g., https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14624
- I encourage the authors to explore the expressiveness and empirical quality of other structural/positional encodings such as Laplacian positional encodings or random-walk structural encodings. A broad overview of common encodings is given in Rampasek et al. 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The theoretical framework of the GT-test is an interesting, although somewhat incremental, perspective on the expressive power of GNNs, in particular graph transformers. However, the augmentation of the WL-test with structural information to increase expressiveness can already be found in [3]. This work simply applies this concept to structural information used in graph Transformers like Graphormer. Theorem 2 was already proven in [4] under a different theoretical framework. Further, Theorem 4 is not new and widely known in the theory community, see, e.g., https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14624

The authors propose a new structural encoding scheme, inspired by the established theory, that improves over their baselines, however, I believe a fair comparison with structural/positional encodings beyond SGD and Neighbor would greatly benefit this work (see also suggestions).

As a minor comment on clarity, I find the name "GT-test" misleading, as the test covers architectures other than the Graph Transformer. What actually distinguishes this test from the WL-test is the additional use of structural encodings. I believe this distinction should be highlighted more.

**References:**

[1] Morris et al. 2018 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02244)

[2] Rampasek et al. 2022 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12454)

[3] Morris et al. 2020 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.01543)

[4] Kreuzer et al. 2021 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03893)
content.summary_of_the_review:
The authors provide an interesting framework for analyzing graph transformers, which, however, is more related to the structural encodings graph transformer tokens are typically augmented with than with graph Transformers per see. 

Nonetheless, the paper presents an interesting result with regard to the expressive power of recently proposed graph Transformer variants: Namely, their expressiveness comes solely from the added structural/positional encodings and not from architectural properties of self-attention. However, this result already follows from known results in the theory community; see above. 

The work could benefit from an extended discussion of various popular structural/positional encodings, as well as experimental results thereof.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer QG9Z, Part 2
content.comment:
> However, the augmentation of the WL-test with structural information to increase expressiveness can already be found in [3]. This work simply applies this concept to structural information used in graph Transformers like Graphormer.

In our view, though GT test adopts the idea of using global and structural information to enhance the expressiveness of graph isomorphism tests, we believe GT test is significantly different from previous methods since it considers different structural information globally and can exhibit an extremely wide range of expressive power with various structural encodings (with *id* it only distinguishes graphs of different sizes; with *Neighbor* it equals to WL; with *SPIS* it distinguishes types of SRGs and is more powerful than 3-WL to some extent.).

> Theorem 2 was already proven in [4] under a different theoretical framework.

Though Theorem 2 in our paper and Theorem 2 in [https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03893] may seem similar, we have to argue that the two results are completely different. Using notations from our paper, The theorem in [https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03893] only considers the network taking absolute structural encoding as input, but our theorem incorporates the case when relative structural encodings like SPD are fed into the Transformer network via attention biases, which greatly increases the difficulty of proving the theorem and extends our theory to GT test with the important relative structural encodings.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer QG9Z, Part 1
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful and constructive comments. In the following we try to answer the question you propose and address your concerns.

> Since the main practical contribution of this work is the SPIS encoding, it would be interesting to see how the encoding fares with Transformer approaches other than Graphormer.

Thanks for your suggestions. Theoretically we have discussed some Transformer approaches in Appendix D, and in experiments we can explain the motivation for choosing Graphormer here: As our whole paper focuses on the theoretical aspect, the goal of our benchmark experiments is to verify that stronger structural encodings can lead to better benchmark performance in real graph Transformers, with the chosen models corresponding to our theory. Therefore, we pick Graphormer because (i) Graphormer proposes SPD which we have conducted research into and has expressivity stronger than WL; (ii) the way Graphormer introduces relative structural encodings perfectly corresponds to our Theorem 2 which is built on a simple Transformer network incorporating relative encodings via attention biases.

However, considering the feedback, we are planning to add more Transformers like GraphGPS into comparison. We look forward to share the results.

> The experiment results should be extended to MPNNs augmented with the discussed structural encodings, as the proposed GT-test is not limited to Transformers.

This is an intuitive question, but we can explain why we do not discuss MPNNs augmented with the discussed structural encoding here: As we have discussed in Section 1-3, from this paper's view, what makes graph Transformers different from MPNNs is the *global* receptive field, then the structural encoding designed for graph Transformers may lose expressivity when applied to locality-based MPNNs. For example, since SPD describes the distance between every node pair in the graph, to inject SPD to MPNNs, for node $v$ in $G=(V,E)$ the model must consider every node in $V$ along with its distance to $v$ to generate the final representation of $v$ (Theorem 1), leading to the contradiction with most existing MPNN architectures which do not exploit both global receptive field and global relative structural encodings (including https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.01543 you mention). On the contrary, the self-attention of Transformers naturally aggregates the global information in this way, so the expressivity of global relative structural encodings (SPD and SPIS) can only be exhibited when equipped by  graph Transformers (or models follow Theorem 1). We can conclude that though GT test is not limited to Transformers, its optimal expressivity can only be demonstrated by Transformers-like models.

> The proposed GT test is more or less the standard 1-WL as used in the theory community, which considers neighbors as well as non-neighbors. The 1-WL as used in the ML community is actually called color refinement; see, e.g., https://people.cs.umass.edu/~immerman/pub/opt.pdf.

Thanks for the useful suggestions. Most of the authors come from the ML community, so we follow the definition of 1-WL from existing works like https://openreview.net/pdf?id=uxgg9o7bI_3. We will add more notes and clarification on this aspect.

> Theorem 4 is not new and widely known in the theory community, see, e.g., https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14624

We sincerely thank your comment. We have read the paper and seen that Theorem 4 is mathematically equivalent to its Theorem VIII.8, but we obtained this theorem independently under the GT test framework. We will add citations and more discussion here.

> I encourage the authors to explore the expressiveness and empirical quality of other structural/positional encodings such as Laplacian positional encodings or random-walk structural encodings. A broad overview of common encodings is given in Rampasek et al. 2022.

Theoretically, we have studied Laplacian positional encodings in Appendix D, and from our perspective it is difficult to study the random-walk structural encodings using deterministic isomorphism tests including GT test. The expressive power of these encodings cannot be directly compared with shortest-path encodings we focus, so we do not include them in the main paper.

As for empirical experiments, since this paper is theoretically-oriented, we initially perform experiments only on structural encodings discussed in the main paper. If all possible encodings are included for the comparison, the theoretical and experimental parts of the paper may not correspond well. Still, according to your suggestions, we are now trying to add Laplacian positional encodings or random-walk structural encodings to experiments.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a graph isomorphism test algorithm, named GT test. The proposed graph isomorphism algorithm can describe the expressive power of graph Transformers based on the absolute and relative positional encoding. Using the proposed tool, the authors characterize the expressive power of several popular graph Transformer variants. Furthermore, under the instruction of GT test, a strong relative structural encoding method, named SPIS encoding, is introduced. Experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks verify the strengths of the proposed methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ Understanding the representation ability of graph Transformer through structural encodings is interesting and important
+ The overall presentation is clear and the idea is easy to follow.

Weaknesses:
- The writing is poor. Several fundamental issues include:
  1. The definition of structural encodings is not clear. This problem is ill-defined on graphs but no rigorous mathematical definition is given in this work. In particular, it is not clear what are differences between absolute and relative structural encodings (c.f. Definition 2.1).
  2. The authors deliberately address their contribution with very strong emotional words, such as "profound representational abilities" and "extraordinary expressive power" which is too good to be true.
  3. Theorem 2 is not straightforward to understand. It is unclear what is its theoretical or empirical implications.
  4. What does it mean by converging faster when testing graphs? I assume there is no need to retrain the model during the test phase.
  * Other incorrect / weird claims include:
    1. "vanilla self-attention is ignorant of node ordering" in Page 1: the vanilla graph convolutions are also ignorant of node ordering since the node representations have to be equivariant to node ordering
    2. "the expressivity of GT test can be approximated at any precision" in Page 2: how the expressivity be approximated?
    3. The claims "most theoretically powerful graph Transformers" and "expressive capacity of graph Transformers" (Page 4) seem to be conflict with each other and are not intuitive.
- The scope of this study is very limited. This paper does not discuss the self-attention on the fully connected graph that Transformers operate on, but only focus on the expressive power of structural encodings. Therefore the "GT test" is very misleading as it is not limited to Transformer at all. The authors also merely discuss three encoding schemes which are too narrow. Other representative encoding schemes include Laplacian positional encodings or distance encodings are not discussed. It is not clear whether the graph Transformers can benefit from the absolute positional encoding. This renders the title "On the structural expressive power" an overclaim. 
- The novelty is also limited. Existing results on the WL hierarchy are not discussed at all (despite in Proposition 3 but no context regarding high-order WL tests are given). I completely disagree with the claim that "existing MPGNNs are different from graph Transformers". In fact, the expressive power of structural encodings (and a board class of augmentation techniques) can be understood through the analogy of local algorithms and node identities. I recommend the authors to read the survey paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.07697) on relevant theoretical results. Moreover, it feels to me that since graph Transformers have to compute additional information at extra overhead (e.g., O(n^3) for the shortest path encoding), directly comparing its representation ability with 1-WL test is not fair. Therefore (1-)WL tests are not powerful is an underclaim in the context of comparing GT with MPGNNs (1-WL test). Also, given its large memory and time complexity, a tradeoff between expressiveness and complexity should be discussed.
- Experiments are not convincing. Improvements are marginal and all the datasets are of very limited scale. Please compare the proposed approach on open graph benchmarks.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is easy to follow. Many claims in this work needs further justification. Existing results on expressiveness of MPGNN with node identities are not discussed and thus the novelty is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes GT test to characterize the expressive power of graph Transformers. Although the reviewer agrees this is an interesting problem but there are many flaws in the current manuscript that need to be fixed, especially the lack of discussion on existing results, limited scope, and unconvincing experimental results. Therefore, I would like to vote for rejecting the paper.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer CRWf, Part 3
content.comment:
> Moreover, it feels to me that since graph Transformers have to compute additional information at extra overhead (e.g., O(n^3) for the shortest path encoding), directly comparing its representation ability with 1-WL test is not fair. Therefore (1-)WL tests are not powerful is an underclaim in the context of comparing GT with MPGNNs (1-WL test). Also, given its large memory and time complexity, a tradeoff between expressiveness and complexity should be discussed.

We have discussed the complexity issue and the tradeoff between expressiveness and complexity in Appendix C and F. Given the $O(E)$ complexity of WL iterations, almost every approach to improve the theoretical expressivity of the graph model is accompanied by an increase in complexity, like Laplacian positional encoding, random-walk encoding and high order WL GNNs. Therefore, we have compared the proposed SPIS-GT against both WL and the much stronger SPD-GT, while the both methods has almost $O(n^3)$ complexity (see Appendix C).

> Experiments are not convincing. Improvements are marginal and all the datasets are of very limited scale. Please compare the proposed approach on open graph benchmarks.

In the selected datasets we can observe that the performance gains from SPIS is consistent, which can well correspond to our theoretical results. We cannot reproduce the Graphormer experiments on ogb datasets due to the lack of GPUs (it requires 8 V100 GPUs while we only have two 3090 GPUs), so initially we have not included the experiments on ogb datasets. However, according to your comments we are considering adding more experiments on datasets with a larger scale. We look forward to share the results.

display_title: Author Response to Reviewer CRWf, Part 2

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer CRWf, Part 2
content.comment:
> The claims "most theoretically powerful graph Transformers" and "expressive capacity of graph Transformers" (Page 4) seem to be conflict with each other and are not intuitive.

We are sorry if we have caused confusion here and we will try to explain it again. Considering that (1) the expressivity upper bound of graph Transformers is GT test; (2) GT test can be arbitrarily approximated by a simple bias-GT network, so it is one of the most theoretically powerful graph Transformers; (3) bias-GT can be viewed as a simplification of existing graph Transformers like Graphormer, we can conclude that one can characterize the expressive capacity of graph Transformers by understanding the expressivity of GT test.

> The scope of this study is very limited. This paper does not discuss the self-attention on the fully connected graph that Transformers operate on, but only focus on the expressive power of structural encodings. Therefore the "GT test" is very misleading as it is not limited to Transformer at all.

We are sorry that we cannot fully understand your comment here; as we have discussed in Section 1-3, since self-attention is ignorant of structure and treat the graph as "fully connected", the expressive power of structural encodings determines the expressive power of graph Transformers, so we reasonably focus on studying the expressive power of structural encodings. And in Section 3.1 we have mentioned that GT test is not limited and characterizes a wide range of graph neural models that leverage graph structure as a soft inductive bias, but in this paper we focus using it as a theoretical tool to study graph Transformers.

> The authors also merely discuss three encoding schemes which are too narrow. Other representative encoding schemes include Laplacian positional encodings or distance encodings are not discussed. 

We have discussed Laplacian positional encodings in Appendix D. As for distance encodings, we choose shortest path distance encoding as a major example.

> It is not clear whether the graph Transformers can benefit from the absolute positional encoding. 

Generally, an absolute encoding can enhance graph Transformers as long as it contains useful structural information. For example, Appendix D shows that absolute encoding like Laplacian can improve the expressivity of graph Transformers. And ablation studies in [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.05234.pdf] show that degree absolute encoding can improve the performance of Transformers.

> The novelty is also limited. Existing results on the WL hierarchy are not discussed at all (despite in Proposition 3 but no context regarding high-order WL tests are given).

We have discussed existing k-WL GNNs in Appendix B. Additionally, a thorough comparison of GT test and high-order WL could be lengthy and may lose the focus of this paper (the expressivity of graph Transformers).

> I completely disagree with the claim that "existing MPGNNs are different from graph Transformers". In fact, the expressive power of structural encodings (and a board class of augmentation techniques) can be understood through the analogy of local algorithms and node identities. I recommend the authors to read the survey paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.07697) on relevant theoretical results.

We have discussed existing theoretical results on strucrtural encodings for MPGNNs in Appendix B. As we have discussed in Section 1-3, from this paper's view, what makes graph Transformers different from MPGNNs is the *global* receptive field, which is foundamentally different from locality-based message passing. Therefore, although structural encodings can be applied to both MPNNs and graph Transformers, structural encodings for global Transformers can have better capabilities and can not be fully understood via the framework of MPGNNs since they do not follow the aggregation scheme in Theorem 1. For example, since SPD describes the distance between every node pair in the graph, to inject SPD to MPGNNs, for node $v$ in $G=(V,E)$ the model must consider every node in $V$ along with its distance to $v$ to generate the final representation of $v$ (Theorem 1), leading to contradiction with most existing MPGNN architectures which do not exploit both global receptive field and global relative structural encodings. Consequently, the theoretical results in this paper on SPD and proposed SPIS rely on the proposed GT test framework, and cannot be obtained using MPGNN-based methods including those in the paper you recommend.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2916 by Reviewer CRWf
display_title: Author Response to Reviewer CRWf, Part 1

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer CRWf, Part 1
content.comment:
Thank you for your constructive feedback, and in the following we will try to address it point by point. We hope that our answer may clear up some misunderstandings, solve key questions and convince you of the novelty and soundness of our contribution.

>The definition of structural encodings is not clear. This problem is ill-defined on graphs but no rigorous mathematical definition is given in this work. In particular, it is not clear what are differences between absolute and relative structural encodings (c.f. Definition 2.1).

We apologize if our notations have caused any confusion, and we will make some clarification here. Structural encodings in this paper are functions that map individual nodes or node pairs to numerical vectors by leveraging structural information in graph. In this sense, for $G=(V,E)$, an absolute structural encoding $f_A$ is a function that maps $(v,G)$ to the structural representation of $v\in V$, and relative structural structural encoding $f_R$ is also a function that maps $(v,u,G)$ to the structural representation of node pair $(v,u)\in V\times V$, like our examples in Section 4.1. Therefore, the key difference between absolute and relative structural encoding is that absolute encoding generates the representation of *individual nodes*, while the relative one generates that of *node pairs (2-tuples)*. From our perspective, this definition is clear and can support our mathematical work in the next sections of this paper. The soundness of this definition is also not questioned by other reviewers.

> The authors deliberately address their contribution with very strong emotional words, such as "profound representational abilities" and "extraordinary expressive power" which is too good to be true.

We are sorry that these claims can be overstated to some extent, and we will fill fix them in the next revision. However, we believe it is resonable to say that GT test can exhibit strong expressive power given our theoretical results in Section 5 and synthetic experiments in Section 6: SPIS-GT is strictly more powerful than WL and SPD-GT; SPIS-GT distinguishes SRGs with different parameters; SPIS-GT distinguishes 3-WL failure cases, etc.

> Theorem 2 is not straightforward to understand. It is unclear what is its theoretical or empirical implications.

We acknowledge that Theorem 2 is not straightforward to understand given its complexity, and we have summarized its theoretical implications in Section 3.1: *Under certain conditions, Theorem 2 guarantees that the simple Transformer network bias-GT is theoretically capable of capturing structural knowledge introduced as attention biases and arbitrarily approximating its expressivity upper bound*, which leads to the key conclusion that *one can translate the central problem of characterizing the expressive capacity of graph Transformers into understanding the expressivity of GT test, determined by the design of structural encodings*. As for detailed mathematical explanations and proof, we leave it in Appendix A.2 to save space for the main paper.

> What does it mean by converging faster when testing graphs? I assume there is no need to retrain the model during the test phase.

This point comes from a purely theoretical perspective, that the number of iterations until convergence is also important for analyzing graph isomorphism tests. For example, if $G_1$ and $G_2$ can be tested as non-isomorphic by WL in at least 3 iterations but only 1 iterations for SPIS-GT, then SPIS-GT converges faster on this graph pair. With smaller number of iterations SPIS-GT exhibits stronger distinguishing power and is more efficient at testing graphs.

> "vanilla self-attention is ignorant of node ordering" in Page 1: the vanilla graph convolutions are also ignorant of node ordering since the node representations have to be equivariant to node ordering

We will fix this to "vanilla self-attention is ignorant of graph structure" in the next revision. Originally, our statement here is to demonstrate the well-known fact that without structural (positional) encoding, self-attention in Transformer can only treat input tokens equally and is not capable of capturing structural relations, like node odering in NLP.

> "the expressivity of GT test can be approximated at any precision" in Page 2: how the expressivity be approximated?

In Theorem 2, $f_t$ is the GT test function, $g$ is a Transformer, and we prove that $f_t$ can be approximated by $g$ at any precision $\epsilon$ measured by $d_p$ distance.
